name: Brown Grey
lede: Brown grey is a descriptive name for a greyed brown, and its history is the history of dull cloth.

sections.title: A descriptive name
sections.body:
None of the books we hold defines brown grey as a named color. It is a compound of two plain words, and Batchelor notes that both grey and brown can be described as mixtures of other colors, brown as a darkish yellow and grey as a mix of black and white [1]. It sits between [[brown]] and [[grey]]. The swatch is close to [[taupe]], [[stone]] and [[russet]].

Medieval writers did not treat these colors as striking. Pastoureau notes that browns and greys were rare in Florentine dress in the 1340s next to greens and blues [2].

sections.title: Dull cloth
sections.body:
St Clair says fourteenth-century sumptuary laws reserved russet, then a duller brown-grey shade, for people in the meanest occupations such as carters and oxherds [3]. Before true black dyeing came in about 1360, cloth intended as black often came out as dirty brown-greys [3].

Pastoureau notes that the Dutch painter Frans Rijckhals reduced his seventeenth-century barn interiors essentially to browns, beiges, greys and whites [4]. Rothko turned to blacks, browns, greys and deep maroons in later work, to keep viewers from admiring decorative color [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is one of the most common colors in our archive: 3,688 of 23,781 paintings, 15.51 percent, as photographed [6]. It peaks in the 1800s, in 860 of 8,345 paintings [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 40 percent of 2,309 paintings [6]. The most devoted painter is Giovanni di Paolo, in 7 of 12 works here [6]. Aged varnish browns many colors, so some of this is the varnish [6].

notes.cite: St Clair, The Secret Lives of Colour, chs. 105 and 116
